sections.title: Naming a goal as its own clause
sections.content: *azért, hogy* ("in order that, so that") explains WHY you do something, by naming the goal as its own *hogy*-clause — and just like wanting-clauses, that goal clause takes -jon/-jen, because it's a not-yet-real outcome you're working toward, not a plain fact. *Korán kelek, azért, hogy elérjem a vonatot* literally reads "I get up early, for the purpose that I catch the train" — natural English just says "so that I catch the train" or "in order to catch the train."

sections.title: azért, hogy...
rows: Korán kelek, azért, hogy elérjem a vonatot.
I get up early so that I catch the train.
Sokat gyakorlok, azért, hogy fejlődjön a magyar tudásom.
I practice a lot so that my Hungarian improves.
Spórolok, azért, hogy megvalósuljon az álmom.
I save money so that my dream comes true.

items.spanish: Minden nap gyakorlok, azért, hogy magabiztosabb legyek.
items.english: I practice every day so that I become more confident.

items.spanish: Azért dolgozom keményen, hogy sikerüljön a projektem.
items.english: I work hard so that my project succeeds.

sections.content: *azért* and *hogy* don't have to sit side by side — *Azért dolgozom keményen, hogy sikerüljön a projektem* front-loads *azért* right after the reason-carrying verb, with *hogy* opening the purpose clause later in the sentence. Both orders are common; *hogy* always marks where the purpose clause itself begins.
